opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's held up remarkably well, honestly. The winning approach was nnU-Net from Fabian Isensee and the team at the German Cancer Research Center, and what was striking at the time, and still is, is that it wasn't some exotic new architecture. It was essentially a well-engineered U-Net with a very careful, self-configuring pipeline: it looked at the properties of each dataset, things like voxel spacing, image size, and modality, and then automatically made sensible decisions about preprocessing, patch size, network depth, training schedule, and post-processing.

That was really the whole point of the Decathlon. We wanted to know whether you could build one method that generalizes across very different tasks, from brain tumors on multi-parametric MRI to small structures like the pancreas or hepatic vessels on CT, without a human hand-tuning everything for each new problem. nnU-Net showed that you could, and it did it convincingly.

Looking back, I'd say its biggest contribution was almost a methodological lesson for the field. A lot of papers at the time were proposing architectural tweaks and claiming improvements, and nnU-Net showed that a lot of the performance comes from getting the "boring" details right: normalization, resampling, augmentation, ensembling. It became the baseline that everyone has to beat, and for years many fancier approaches, including some transformer-based ones, struggled to consistently outperform it when compared fairly.

Of course, it has limitations. It's computationally heavy, it's still fundamentally a supervised method that depends on good annotations, and it doesn't address the harder clinical questions on its own, like uncertainty, robustness to scanner shifts, or what to do with very rare pathologies. And now there's a lot of excitement around foundation models and more general-purpose segmentation tools. But I'd still say nnU-Net is one of the clearest examples of a challenge producing something that genuinely changed practice, and that's exactly what we hoped the Decathlon would do.

r001.rationale: The response says nnU-Net has held up well and remains a baseline that many newer approaches struggle to outperform fairly. It does not clearly state that it still generally performs best across a broad range of segmentation tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The winning method from the original Decathlon was nnU-Net, from Fabian Isensee and Klaus Maier-Hein's group, and I think it has aged remarkably well. Honestly, it reshaped how a lot of us think about the field.

What's striking is that it didn't win on architectural novelty. It was a fairly plain U-Net. What it got right was everything around the network: automatically configuring preprocessing, patch size, resampling, normalization, and the training recipe from the properties of the dataset itself. That was the real insight of the challenge. We had deliberately designed the Decathlon so that nobody could hand-tune a method to ten different tasks, and nnU-Net showed that a principled, self-configuring pipeline generalizes better than clever architectures tuned to one problem.

Looking at it today, a few things stand out. First, it's still a very hard baseline to beat. Years later, many papers claiming improvements turn out to be within the noise of a well-configured nnU-Net, and that has been a healthy, humbling lesson about how we evaluate methods. Second, it pushed the community toward reproducibility. It shipped as usable software, not just a paper, and that's a big part of why it became the default.

Where I'd be more critical is that its success may have slowed exploration in some directions. Foundation models and promptable segmentation, things like SAM-style approaches adapted to medical imaging, are finally offering a genuinely different paradigm, and they're still being measured against nnU-Net. It also doesn't solve the problems we care most about clinically: domain shift across scanners and institutions, rare pathologies, and uncertainty estimation. Those weren't really what the Decathlon measured.

So my assessment is that it was the right winner, it exposed how much of our progress was engineering rather than modeling, and the field's next step is to ask harder questions than the ones that benchmark could pose.

r001.rationale: The response says nnU-Net remains a very hard baseline to beat and that many claimed improvements fall within noise, but does not clearly state that it generally performs best across a broad range of segmentation tasks.

astra-6.text: I think its lasting contribution is showing how much you can achieve by getting the whole pipeline right. The winning method, nnU-Net, wasn’t simply a new network architecture; it adapted preprocessing, training, and other choices to the dataset. It remains a strong baseline. But winning a segmentation benchmark is different from demonstrating clinical value. I’d also want to know how it performs on data from another hospital, where it fails, and whether it actually helps clinicians.

r001.rationale: It calls nnU-Net a strong baseline, but does not state that it still generally performs best across a broad range of segmentation tasks.

sol-6.1.text: I think the lasting lesson is that getting the whole pipeline right matters enormously. The winning method, nnU-Net, showed how far you could go with a well-configured U-Net, careful preprocessing, and training choices that adapted to the dataset, rather than a radically new architecture. I still see that as a strong baseline. But success on a benchmark is only part of the picture; you also want to know how a method performs on data from a different hospital and whether its errors are clinically meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response calls nnU-Net a strong baseline and praises its pipeline, but does not state that it still generally performs best across a broad range of segmentation tasks.
